why: Nothing shows intended scope versus files actually touched; the user would have to scroll the transcript and cross-check git status per session, which nobody does reliably. Catching drift early avoids reverting an hour of wrong work, so it changes a real decision often.

Answering is easy once you know which tab is asking: switch pane, type, enter, well under 30 seconds. The value is removing a context switch you make dozens of times a day, not unblocking something otherwise impossible.

No harness aggregates headroom; you would run /usage in Claude, squint at the Codex usage line, and still have no forward projection to combine them into a yes or no. A wrong call means a long job dies at the wall, so the answer changes what you launch.

The blocked prompt is literally on screen in that harness pane, so it is tedium not inaccessibility, but catching it means polling 3 to 12 panes repeatedly and no harness pushes it. An agent sitting idle waiting on a one-word answer is direct wasted wall-clock time, every day.

No harness estimates turn duration at all, so there is nothing to read and nothing to combine; a single next-needed time is not derivable by hand. It converts a vague hover into a concrete decision to leave the desk, though it rests on estimates the user will only half trust.

Reachable with effort: each pane shows its own cwd, and tmux list-panes or ps can enumerate them, but you have to think to check and nothing warns you. Two agents editing the same repo clobbers work, which is concrete loss rather than inconvenience.

No harness keeps queryable history of interruptions, so reconstructing where your attention went would mean scraping session files across harnesses and over days. Genuinely unobtainable, but it is a retrospective argument rather than something that changes what you do next.

Requires remembering which finished outputs you already read, correlating across sessions and across time, which is exactly the thing people fail at. Collecting a completed result you forgot about recovers work already paid for, and it happens weekly.

Stake is not displayed anywhere and is not really derivable; the user half-knows it from memory of what they asked, and reconstructing it across ten sessions is manual. Useful for ordering triage, but it is an inferred label most users will not trust enough to override their own instinct.

One command in Claude Code: /usage reports the window and reset, and anyone running a status-line tool like Barista sees it without asking. Knowing you have 12 percent left before a long refactor genuinely changes whether you start it, so it earns its keep despite being cheap to obtain.
